title: Part 1
text: Why does the idea of eating human flesh turn your stomach before you even think about it? Biology may have part of the answer.

title: Part 2
text: Many researchers think disgust is not just a mood. They describe it as a kind of behavioral immune system.
nxt: It pushes you away from things that carry disease: rotten food, waste, sickness.

title: Part 3
text: Here is a thought experiment, and to be clear, it is an imagined scenario, not a record of real people. Picture two groups of early humans, hundreds of thousands of years ago.

title: Part 4
text: Group A has no strong aversion to eating their dead. Group B feels an overwhelming revulsion.
nxt: Over many generations, which group would you expect to suffer more from prion disease and infection? In this story, Group A is hit harder, and Group B stays healthier.

title: Part 5
text: There is another benefit. A group that refuses to treat its members as food can build deeper trust.
nxt: People who see one another as allies, not emergency rations, can hunt together and raise children together. Disgust, empathy, and taboo may have supported each other.

title: Part 6
text: Genetics adds one more clue. In 2003, a team led by the researcher Simon Mead studied a gene called PRNP, which makes the prion protein.
nxt: At position 129, people carry one of two versions. Those with one of each, called heterozygotes, seemed better protected. Among Fore women who had survived kuru, most were heterozygous.

title: Part 7
text: The team then looked at populations around the world.
nxt: They found that both versions are common in many regions, and they argued that this balance may reflect natural selection, perhaps from deadly kuru-like epidemics in the distant past.

title: Part 8
text: So treat it as a fascinating possibility. The taboo is also cultural, and cultures differ.
nxt: But beneath the stories we tell, there may be a quiet biological logic.
